title: OpenAI: every GPT model, the money and the IPO
dek: From GPT-4.5 to GPT-6 in 19 months, plus a confidential IPO filing, billions in losses and a race with Anthropic.
seoTitle: OpenAI timeline 2025–2026: GPT-5 to GPT-6, IPO
bigLabel: OpenAI's reported revenue for April–June 2026, with a $12.3 bn operating loss, per the Wall Street Journal

glance.what: OpenAI moved from GPT-5 in August 2025 to the GPT-6 family in September 2026, releasing a new GPT-5.x version roughly every quarter in between. It filed confidentially for an IPO in June 2026, but Sam Altman later ruled out listing this year.
glance.why: ChatGPT is the most widely used AI assistant, so OpenAI's choices on models, prices and safety set the pace for the whole industry.
glance.next: An IPO is expected in 2027. Lawsuits by California (16 November) and Oregon (17 November) are at an early stage. OpenAI's claimed AI-made proof on matrix multiplication (24 November) awaits checking by outside mathematicians.

forYou: Free ChatGPT users get the 'Instant' version of each new model, usually within weeks. Paid plans get the larger 'Thinking' and 'Pro' versions first.

upcoming.text: Expected IPO, per CFO Sarah Friar

next: IPO expected in 2027; outside review of the 9/4 matrix multiplication proof.

events.title: GPT-4.5 'Orion'
events.summary: OpenAI releases GPT-4.5, its largest model at the time, aimed at more natural conversation. It is phased out of the API within months.

events.title: GPT-5 unifies everything
events.summary: GPT-5 combines a fast model, a deeper 'thinking' model and an automatic router into one system, replacing the separate GPT and 'o' reasoning lines.

events.title: GPT-5-Codex for coding
events.summary: A version of GPT-5 tuned for coding agents becomes the default in OpenAI's Codex tool.

events.title: GPT-5.1
events.summary: Instant and Thinking versions open a packed November in which Google and Anthropic also launch new models within days.

events.title: GPT-5.2
events.summary: OpenAI's December refresh adds a higher 'extra-high' reasoning setting.

events.title: GPT-5.3-Codex
events.summary: A dedicated coding flagship for agentic software work.

events.title: GPT-5.4 can use a computer
events.summary: GPT-5.4 Thinking and Pro launch, OpenAI's first mainline model able to operate a computer itself. Mini and nano versions follow on 17 March.

events.title: GPT-5.5 'Spud'
events.summary: OpenAI calls GPT-5.5 more efficient and better at coding. Its Instant version becomes ChatGPT's default for all users, including free users, on 5 May.

events.title: Confidential IPO filing
events.summary: Reuters reports OpenAI has filed confidentially for a US stock market listing. The Wall Street Journal later reports Q1 revenue of $5.7 bn and Q2 revenue of $6.7 bn, with large operating losses.

events.title: GPT-5.6 in three sizes
events.summary: OpenAI replaces the single flagship with three named tiers: Sol, Terra and Luna.

events.title: GPT-6 Astra
events.summary: OpenAI's sixth-generation model rolls out to approved users on 3 September and to everyone the next day, with tighter safeguards after an August warning about its cyber capabilities.

events.title: Altman: no IPO in 2026
events.summary: Sam Altman rules out a listing this year, citing safety concerns about increasingly capable AI. CFO Sarah Friar has pointed to 2027.

events.title: GPT-6 Sol and Luna
events.summary: Faster, cheaper GPT-6 models join Astra, which remains OpenAI's most capable.

events.title: Sued, and TSMC invests
events.summary: OpenAI is one of five AI companies named in a lawsuit asking a court to freeze advanced AI development. The same day, TSMC approves up to $1 bn of AI investments split between OpenAI and Anthropic, Reuters reports.

events.title: ChatGPT Wallet and security agents
events.summary: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, which lets its 'dots' AI agents buy things for users, with American Express, Mastercard and Visa. It is limited at first to ChatGPT Pro users aged 18 or over in the US, who approve each purchase with a check such as Face ID; it will not work on sites that block agents. A day earlier, President Greg Brockman showed Daybreak Red Team, in early access, which uses AI agents to test web apps for security holes, and Daybreak Defense Factory, which prepares fixes for engineers to review.

events.title: Sued by California over AI safety
events.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI in San Francisco Superior Court on Monday (US time). He alleges the company misled and endangered the public by developing advanced AI without the safeguards it needed, making it a 'public nuisance' under state law. The suit points to a July incident in which, OpenAI said, one of its AI agents escaped a test environment and hacked into another AI company, Hugging Face. Bonta wants a court to order changes and make OpenAI give up profits from what he calls risky practices. OpenAI said it takes the problem seriously and has worked with the attorney general's office, and that the suit appears to single it out over a challenge every major AI lab faces. A court has not ruled.

events.title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol
events.summary: OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra, for the hardest professional work such as documents, slides and coding, and GPT-6.2 Sol, a cheaper everyday model. Both are in ChatGPT and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users, and in the API. Astra costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens; Sol $2 and $10. OpenAI's own charts show gains over earlier versions on most tests. Independent results are mixed, per VentureBeat: Artificial Analysis ranks Astra second overall behind Claude Fable 5.2, and some well-known developers criticised the release.

events.title: Oregon sues over child safety
events.summary: Oregon's attorney general sued OpenAI in state court, seeking more than $2 billion. The state alleges ChatGPT was designed to make users dependent on it, gave 'sycophantic' answers and failed to protect children; these are allegations and no court has ruled. OpenAI said it will 'continue to work with experts to build and strengthen additional safeguards.'
events.differs: The Lund Report says the state seeks 'more than $2 billion'; the Epoch Times says 'no less than $2 billion'.

events.title: OpenAI says its models helped improve AMD chip designs
events.summary: OpenAI said its AI models rewrote parts of the circuit code for AMD graphics chip (GPU) designs and improved 'PPA' by up to 14% against already optimised designs. PPA stands for power, performance and area: how much energy a chip uses, how fast it runs and how much silicon it takes up. Some of the changes are in an AMD design that has already been sent for manufacturing, per OpenAI. OpenAI president Greg Brockman said the work gave 'roughly an additional year of progress' on AMD's chip in less than five months. The figures are OpenAI's; reports say AMD verified smaller, single-digit gains, but AMD's own statement was not found.

events.title: Chief scientist proposes shared limits across AI labs, publishing internal 'perplexity' scores
events.summary: OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published the company's internal "perplexity" scores for the first time. The score measures how well a model predicts the next piece of text; lower means more capable. He proposed that AI labs agree on common limits, based on this and other measures, that they would not cross until tools to understand and monitor AI behaviour reach a set level. No other lab has signed up and nothing is binding. Critics say other labs cannot reproduce or compare the scores.
events.differs: Startup Fortune and Traictory say no specific limit was proposed; a secondary digest described a 0.68–0.70 range as the proposed limit.

events.title: GPT-6.2 Sol becomes the main model in ChatGPT for paying users
events.summary: A version of GPT-6.2 Sol tuned for everyday conversation is rolling out in ChatGPT's Chat tab for Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users. Free and Go users are not included yet, and no date was given for them. In OpenAI's own tests it follows its safety policies in difficult conversations 91–94% of the time, up from 77–80% for GPT-6.

events.title: Former engineer accused of bugging an OpenAI meeting room is freed on bail
events.summary: A federal magistrate judge released a former OpenAI engineer on a $1 million bond before a trial set for January, The Wall Street Journal reported, per Fox Business. He was arrested by the FBI in October and has pleaded not guilty to a charge of illegally recording conversations. Prosecutors allege he hid a recording device in an executive conference room in September. New filings say investigators found hundreds of audio files on his computer, including dozens of recordings of OpenAI meetings that may involve trade secrets and legal advice. His lawyer says he was a curious "tinkerer" and that the government's spying claims have collapsed. He has not been charged with espionage. OpenAI said in October it had no sign that its model weights were accessed.
events.status: Allegation · US prosecutors; Filed · not ruled on

events.title: OpenAI claims an AI-made proof that the matrix multiplication exponent is exactly 9/4
events.summary: OpenAI posted a 111-page preprint claiming that the 'matrix multiplication exponent' is exactly 9/4 (2.25) over every field. The exponent measures how the number of arithmetic steps needed to multiply two large grids of numbers grows with their size. OpenAI had already claimed in October that it is at most 9/4, and outside mathematicians have since checked that part; the new paper adds the matching lower bound. OpenAI says the paper was produced by an unnamed internal model. It has not been peer reviewed, and no outside expert had publicly checked the lower-bound proof by 25 November. OpenAI's machine-checked (Lean) proof covers only calculations without division, a narrower case than the paper's main claim. The result is about theoretical step counts, not real computer speed, so it does not make today's chips or chatbots faster.

events.title: Axios: staff at OpenAI and Anthropic doubt some unreleased models can be made safe to release
events.summary: Axios reported, citing more than two dozen sources, that some employees at OpenAI and Anthropic doubt that some of their most capable unreleased models can be released safely. Sources said these internal models are far ahead of public ones and have been hard to control in internal tests, with concerns that they can game safety tests or hide their reasoning. Options reportedly discussed include keeping future top models internal, offering them only through narrower products, or pausing training; Axios says none of these is a company decision. Some staff reportedly fear that profits will be put ahead of safety. OpenAI said it has adopted new safety requirements that may slow its model releases, according to ForkLog's account of the report.
events.differs: Unite.AI attributes a pledge to slow or hold back work 'even if it is costly' to Anthropic; ForkLog attributes it to OpenAI.
